li.a: The Spokesman-Review: Brother Speed motorcycle club settles lawsuit with feds over Idaho clubhouse raid
United States District Court for the District of Idaho: Memorandum Decision and Order, 24 November 2014, case 4:14-cv-00172
Motorcycle Profiling Project: Why the Brother Speed MC Victory is So Important
NBC News: 26 outlaw bikers crash on Oregon freeway
California Department of Justice, via the National Criminal Justice Reference Service: Outlaw Motorcycle Gangs USA Overview
Law Tigers: Boise Brother Speed Motorcycle Club Explores Idaho Rides
One Percenter Bikers: Brother Speed MC (Motorcycle Club)

content.p: Brother Speed is a motorcycle club that began in Boise, Idaho, in May 1969 and now has chapters across the northwestern United States. It is one of those clubs that two groups describe in opposite terms. Police intelligence reports and some press coverage have called it an outlaw club, and individual members have faced charges. The club and its lawyer say its members are working tradesmen who were treated as suspects on speculation and assumptions, in the words of the chapter president.

The public record is thin and uneven. There is no conviction of the club as an organisation in the pages opened here. What exists is a scattering of incidents involving individual members, a long-ago law-enforcement intelligence summary, and one well-documented episode in which the state, not the club, was on the defensive: a 2013 raid on a clubhouse that produced no charges and ended in a payment from the federal government.

According to an account published by the motorcycle-accident law firm Law Tigers, the club began as a group of school friends who rode together, and many of their fathers rode as well. A biker-reference website adds that they placed an advertisement to arrange a ride. The firm says the Boise club formed officially in May 1969 and chose the name Brother Speed shortly afterwards.

The club's emblem, a winged skull in a cap and goggles, dates from that period, the firm says, and it remains the centre patch. The club's colours are black and gold. The biker-reference site says the club grew first to Logan, Idaho, and Portland, Oregon, and now has about a dozen chapters in the north-west, with no chapters abroad. It also says the club has a racing arm that competes in drag racing and in speed-record attempts on the salt flats. Law Tigers puts the membership at 200 to 300 but cautions that the real number is hard to know.
Neither source is independent of the biker world, and neither is a history written from club records. They agree on the date and the setting, and that is as far as they can be pressed.

The earliest official mention in the pages opened is in a report produced by the California Department of Justice and circulated by the National Criminal Justice Reference Service. It was prepared for a law-enforcement training seminar, is marked as intended for the restricted use of police, and refers to events in 1990 and 1991, so it dates from the early 1990s. It names Brothers Speed, in that spelling, among the outlaw motorcycle gangs that it said dominated activity in the western United States.

The report goes further, and its claims are those of intelligence analysts, not findings of a court. It says Brothers Speed in Idaho had dealt with members of the Aryan Nations in northern Idaho in buying illegal weapons, and that members and associates were ordering parts and assembling fully automatic stun guns. It says the club in Reno, Nevada, along with the Hells Angels' Sacramento chapter and a California Nomad chapter, was believed to be using twin-engine aircraft to move narcotics between Nevada and northern California. It lists the club in Oregon, Washington and Idaho among groups known to associate with others to obtain precursor chemicals for methamphetamine, and says the club was sending methamphetamine to a club in Sydney, Australia. It adds that the club in Idaho was courting the Bandidos, out of fear that the Hells Angels would take over its operations.

None of these statements is accompanied, in the pages opened, by a name, a case number or an outcome. They show how law enforcement saw the club three decades before the Nampa raid. They do not show what any member was convicted of.

A biker-reference website, One Percenter Bikers, assembles a timeline of episodes. It is a hobbyist site that does not cite its sources, so each item below is attributed to it unless another page is named.

It says a clubhouse in Pocatello, Idaho, was raided in 2005 in a methamphetamine investigation. The property belonged to a member, Ty Chacon, who the site says pleaded guilty to trafficking the drug and was sentenced in 2006 to 23 years in prison for the distribution and for lying in court. The site says he was believed to be a ringleader of methamphetamine distribution in the area. It adds that no other member is famous in a celebrity sense.

The same timeline lists, for April 2012, the arrest of two members over harassment, menacing and reckless driving after a car was chased and struck with a metal hook and with hands. It does not say what became of the charges.

The next month produced a better-documented episode, reported by the Associated Press and carried by CBS News. Rexburg police said nearly 400 bikers had gathered on a Saturday to grant the wish of a seven-year-old cancer patient to take part in a motorcycle rally, when five members of what the report called the Idaho Falls-based Brothers Speed attacked two bikers from the Empties motorcycle club of Pocatello. A 57-year-old Pocatello man suffered serious head and facial injuries and broken bones, and a 50-year-old man had minor injuries. Police said the second man fired a 9 mm pistol in what he said were warning shots meant to break up the fight. The rally went on to raise more than $6,000 toward the boy's medical costs. The report does not say whether anyone was charged.

The One Percenter Bikers timeline also records that on 25 July 2015, after reports of a possible confrontation between Brother Speed and another club at a POW/MIA rally in Bannock County, Idaho, police from several agencies responded, using an armoured vehicle and several tactical teams. The same site says other pages name Vagos and Mongols as the club's enemies but that it found no clear information on whether that is true.

On Friday 18 September 2009 more than two dozen motorcycles went down on Interstate 5 near Wilsonville, south of Portland. NBC News, relaying Oregon State Police, reported that the riders were behind a car when traffic slowed unexpectedly in the northbound lanes and that bikes scattered across the road. A fire official described emergency crews arriving to find "ordered mayhem". The Oregonian, cited by NBC, put the number of bikers at 26 and said two with critical injuries were flown to Portland hospitals; seven others were treated for injuries including broken bones. The freeway reopened nearly four hours later.

Officials said most of the victims belonged to Brother Speed, and NBC reported that the Oregonian said the Oregon Department of Justice identified the group as an outlaw biker gang. The One Percenter Bikers timeline says the riders were on their way to the Portland chapter's annual birthday event and that one of the critically injured riders later died in hospital. That detail comes from that site alone.

The episode with the fullest record began on the night of Wednesday 28 August 2013. The Boise station KBOI reported that the Canyon County Sheriff's Office said federal and local agencies, together with the Treasure Valley Metro Violent Crime Task Force, had served search warrants at three locations in Nampa: the Brother Speed clubhouse, the clubhouse of a club called the Road Brothers, and a private house. A man was arrested at one of them, and the sheriff's office said the warrant was sealed. The Motorcycle Profiling Project, which advocates for riders, also says the warrant was sealed and that nothing was found and no one was charged.

A federal judge's later order supplies the background. The searches were part of the task force's investigation of Timothy Butterbaugh, who was a member of the Road Brothers club. One search warrant, signed by a magistrate judge, named four targets: Butterbaugh's home, the Road Brothers premises, the Brother Speed building and a 1991 Ford Ranger. The Justice Department's announcement of Butterbaugh's arrest said the warrants were served by the FBI, the task force, the Canyon County Sheriff's Office, Nampa police and Meridian police. The Brother Speed plaintiffs believed that the same or very similar information had supported the applications for all four locations. The order quotes the title of that announcement as "Nampa Man Arrested on Federal Drug Charge". The order does not say that any Brother Speed member was a target.

The club's account, as the Spokesman-Review reported it, is that agents broke down the door, set off flash-bang grenades and put dozens of heavily armed tactical officers inside a small house. Members were held for up to three hours while agents removed property, including their clothing, and took club memorabilia, according to the club's attorney, Craig Durham. The Motorcycle Profiling Project, whose founder writes for it as an advocate, says more than 40 officers took part. That figure comes from the project and not from an official source. The court order's background section says the raid was apparently carried out "in a military fashion" with percussion grenades, smoke and "overwhelming numbers", and that officers in riot gear did not identify themselves. The order uses the hedge "apparently" and does not treat these as findings.

Within days a Boise police gang detective who had not been on the raid told local television that clubs such as Brother Speed were different from ordinary weekend riders because of what he called criminal activity. The Motorcycle Profiling Project quotes him and argues that his remarks were stereotype, because nothing was found in the clubhouse. That claim, too, is the project's own.

Twelve club members sued, including the Nampa chapter's president, Daniel Bugli. The defendants were the Canyon County sheriff, Kieran Donahue, an FBI special agent, Douglas Hart, who was added by amendment, Canyon County, the City of Nampa, and unnamed members of the task force and of several agencies. The case was filed in the United States District Court for the District of Idaho.

The court's order of 24 November 2014 shows the early manoeuvring in the case. The county and city defendants had asked for summary judgment before any discovery, saying they had no part in obtaining or serving the warrant. The judge declined for the time being, holding that the plaintiffs had stated a colorable claim and that reports indicated the county and city had partnered with federal officers. The United States, for its part, had asked to intervene in order to stop discovery for six months while a criminal investigation went on. The court allowed it to intervene for that limited purpose and said it was inclined to grant a temporary stay.

The case ended a year later. In November 2015 the Spokesman-Review reported that the government would pay $16,500 to settle: $4,000 to the club and from $500 to $2,500 each to ten members. The government admitted no wrongdoing. Wendy Olson, the United States Attorney for Idaho, said in a statement, reported on the Spokesman-Review's Eye on Boise blog, that the amount was a small fraction of the more than $6 million the plaintiffs had sought, and said the Justice Department often resolves such civil suits for nominal amounts rather than spend more resources. Bugli said the case had never been about money but about citizens' rights. Durham said in the same account that the members were "regular guys minding their own business that night".

In the news release that accompanied the settlement, Durham and Bugli said the Nampa and Caldwell chapter's members were mostly tradesmen, among them a pipe fitter, a tile setter, an electrician and a plumber, and that four were retired. The Spokesman-Review's account of the release goes on to recall 2010, when Idaho's state budget was short, and says members worked with the state parks department to help keep a park in the Magic Valley open; it adds that the Associated Press reported at the time nine bikers in leather jackets bearing the club's grinning skull planting 75 maple trees at Thousand Springs State Park alongside college students, a Mormon group and a square-dance club.

Law Tigers adds that the club's Burley chapter holds an annual toy run to gather Christmas presents for children, and that chapters support raffles and other community events. The firm calls the club controversial and says many sources refer to it as an outlaw club.

The sources do not settle what Brother Speed is. Intelligence summaries from the early 1990s, a state justice department's label as reported in 2009, and a police detective's remarks in 2013 portray an outlaw club. The court records show members as plaintiffs, not defendants, in the one case that reached a judge. Individual members have faced charges, and the pages opened give a guilty plea and sentence for one of them, from a single website that cites no source. The pages also say a raid on the club's own clubhouse found nothing that led to a charge.
